solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: distractors A/C/D are weak; C (seasonal) is the only even slightly tempting one, so the item is very easy
S034-01.notes: The spring keeps flowing even in the driest summers, so the supply seemed inexhaustible. Contaminated and costly don't connect to the flow; seasonal says the opposite.

flags: minor: the only obstacle is knowing the word 'auspicious'; students who don't know it can still get there by eliminating ominous, negligible and ambiguous, which are all negative or neutral
S034-02.notes: Three of four wells struck water and the project could succeed, so the results were promising. Ominous is the opposite; negligible and ambiguous clash with the clear success.

flags: minor: B, C and D are easy to rule out (C brings in modern concrete, B misreads the text, D is too broad)
minor: the facts are accurate (2023 MIT study by Seymour, Masic et al., Science Advances: lime clasts dissolve and recrystallize as calcium carbonate)
S034-03.notes: Lumps once thought to show careless mixing may have let the concrete repair its own cracks.

flags: minor: the facts match the classic Chase & Simon findings, including the small expert edge on random boards
S034-04.notes: The experts' advantage nearly disappears on random boards, so it must come from recognizing meaningful patterns. A is contradicted by the random-board result. B and D are unsupported.

flags: minor: answer cue: B is the only choice that covers both halves of the conclusion and the only one citing all four numbers, so it can be picked without much thought; A and C each address only one half, and D is irrelevant
S034-05.notes: The conclusion has two parts: A's higher median (120 vs 60) and B's longer maximum (900 vs 400). Only B gives both.

flags: minor: the facts are accurate (Mueller & Oppenheimer 2014; replication by Morehead, Dunlosky & Rawson 2019)
minor: C (sample size) is not supported, since Text 2 doesn't discuss sample size
S034-06.notes: Text 2 finds smaller, inconsistent or no differences, so it would say the evidence for a handwriting advantage is weaker than claimed. A and B overstate in opposite directions.

flags: minor: C is the only choice that gives the cause (rejection by U.S. schools), which makes elimination easy
S034-07.notes: The goal is to explain why she went to France. C gives the reason: she was refused by U.S. flight schools.

flags: minor: 'Thus' may tempt quick readers because the second sentence also involves cause and effect, but the move from strengthening to self-weakening is a contrast
minor: the science is accurate (a stalled storm brings up cooler water, which weakens it)
S034-08.notes: Sentence 1 says warm seas strengthen storms; sentence 2 says a stalled storm weakens itself by bringing up cooler water. That is a contrast, so 'Conversely' fits. 'Similarly' and 'For example' don't fit the relationship.

flags: minor: B ('children's choirs performance') is the main trap: a plural noun can't take 'performance' without an apostrophe, so it would need to be 'choirs''
minor: the double possessive in D is correct but sounds odd, which may push students toward B
S034-09.notes: Inserting each choice: 'children's choir's performance' is the only one that marks both possessives correctly. A and C put the apostrophe in the wrong place on 'children'; B leaves 'choirs' without the possessive it needs.

flags: minor: 'thousands of workers had been working ... for about five years' suggests every worker worked all five years; the facts otherwise check out (1931 to 1936)
S034-10.notes: The sentence is set in the past ('By the time... was completed in 1936') and the work continued up to that point, so the past perfect progressive 'had been working' is needed. A and C are present tense; D is future.
